rss_0_1785958843.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
rss_0_1785958843.text:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

rss_1_1785958843.title: El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year
rss_1_1785958843.text:
About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting.

This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices from the war in Iran.

Even if the forecast El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries currently in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Wednesday.

Central and South America, the Caribbean and southern Africa are likely to be worst affected, according to the analysis. In south and south-east Asia there is likely to be less rainfall than usual, which would cause serious problems for agriculture and farmers.

This year’s El Niño – a weather system that develops every few years in the Pacific Ocean and brings changes to rainfall patterns around the world – is shaping up to be the strongest in at least 70 years. Some are calling it a “super El Niño”, though this term is not officially recognised.

What is certain is that its impacts and strength are being strongly affected by the climate crisis. Earlier this year, experts said a strong El Niño could work in tandem with global heating to deliver the hottest year on record either this year or, more likely, in 2027.

Private sector forecasters have already warned of the impact of the gathering El Niño on global food prices, but the report published by the WFP is the first to look closely at global hunger. The WFP said it was hoping to reduce the effects of the extreme weather through early warning systems and “anticipatory” relief efforts, for which at least $80m (£60m) is budgeted.

The consequences will still be far-reaching, as farmers may take more than one season to exhaust their food supplies. In southern Africa, for instance, the main growing season stretches from October this year to March 2027, but it will be about nine months later, during the lean season following the harvest, that the worst impacts will bite.

“The biggest food security impact, in southern Africa, will be during the 2027 to 2028 lean season,” said Richard Choularton, the WFP’s director of the climate and resilience service.

Farmers should be somewhat cushioned by the lingering benefits of last year’s harvest, which was an unusually good one. “At the end of 2025, food prices were in favourable ranges, though there has been upward pressure from the war in the Middle East,” said Jean-Martin Bauer, the WFP’s director of food security.

During the 2015-16 El Niño, about 60 million to 100 million people were affected by acute food insecurity, the term WFP uses to denote hunger that falls below the level of famine. In those years, the WFP was not yet rolling out its updated anticipatory actions, so its experts hope this year’s extreme weather will have a lower impact even if the El Niño is more severe.

However, Choularton said efforts had been hampered by a lack of data, as some collection efforts had been cut for lack of funding.

The WFP’s data covers the 45 countries it works in where baseline estimates for food insecurity are available. There could be additional impacts outside these hard-hit areas.

Food prices could come under pressure across the world, as well as in the 45 countries examined, said Bauer. “This will also depend on the choices that exporting countries make. It’s very important to avoid a situation where large countries stop food exports,” he said. “At the regional level, there could certainly be high prices and [problems with] food access.”

In the UK and Europe, farmers have been warning of the impact of extreme heat and lack of rainfall on their harvests, with retailers braced for higher prices.

rss_2_1785958843.title: Wednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpoint
rss_2_1785958843.text:
Good morning. Last week, an estimated 72,000 migrants began crossing into a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Morocco. Within 24 hours, most of them had headed home. At least 88 people died after attempting the crossing, according to local officials. This isn’t the whole story of what happened over the last week, but the facts are worth remembering.

At an emergency meeting yesterday, EU interior ministers sought to draw a line under Ceuta, insisting that the passport-free Schengen area had never been at risk from the arrival of migrants at this scale. Despite this, much of the media coverage has suggested that events in Ceuta represent a territorial threat to Europe, sparking calls for greater security across the region’s borders.

It’s a pattern that has become familiar since the 2015 refugee crisis. As Europe has created fewer opportunities for migrants to legally cross its borders, people have tried to cross them illegally, resulting in dangerous bottlenecks, human tragedies, and a slew of spectacular images that the right has seized upon to justify draconian policies.

For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to Daniel Trilling, a journalist who writes about refugees and migration, about the political actors trying to capitalise on Ceuta, and why tragedies like this are bound to keep happening. That’s after the headlines.

Five big stories

Environment | Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves. UK politics | Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said, promising a root-and-branch reform of standards after several damning maternity scandals. Middle East | Jordan is convening an emergency meeting over an “imminent” threat of an Israeli takeover of the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”. Ukraine | Russian strikes in and around Kyiv killed at least 14 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Some reports put the death toll at 15. Ceuta | Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

In depth: ‘The claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue’

View image in fullscreen Migrants who crossed into Spain via Ceuta are escorted by the Spanish army back to Morocco. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP

On Thursday, a group of people roughly the size of Guildford’s population began crossing into Ceuta. Many of them swam around the border fence. Some drowned; others were crushed. Dozens died. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you,” one told the Guardian.

Most of these people were young men searching for work and hoping to build a better life for themselves. There are no reports suggesting any of them reached mainland Europe. “It’s very difficult for people without the right documents to travel from Ceuta to mainland Europe, and Spain has lots of experience returning people who cross without permission,” Trilling says. “So the claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue.”

Although Spain was reporting on Friday that most of these migrants had returned to Morocco, videos of men clambering on rocks and walking through Ceuta’s streets had already gone viral on social media, where they were amplified by right-wing voices. “Ceuta has been turned into a third world city in only 48 hours,” Tommy Robinson posted on X. Elon Musk, no stranger to sticking his oar into the politics of foreign nations, posted: “all military age males means it is an invasion”.

“By the time the images started circulating, the so-called crisis was over. But the political damage was already done,” Trilling says.

Why did so many people make the crossing?

A social media hoax, which hinged on a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, seems to have played a pivotal role in encouraging the crossings. Instagram posts suggested Spain’s border with Morocco was opening up, TikTok videos showed people where to swim, and Facebook users began tracking coast guard patrols. It’s unclear who was behind these accounts, as several of them were deleted soon after the crossings. At a crisis meeting on Saturday, EU member states speculated that the events may have been coordinated.

As the hoax spread, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum, allowing thousands of people to cross into Ceuta. Some analysts have suggested that Rabat, Morocco’s administrative capital, deliberately opened the border to protest Pedro Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria (Morocco has a territorial dispute with the country). Others have pointed to Rabat’s increasingly toasty relationship with the Trump administration, which has clashed with Sánchez during the Iran war.

Hasn’t this happened before?

“The central problem is that European border policies have given countries like Morocco a means of exerting pressure on European states,” Trilling says. The EU has increasingly outsourced (“externalised,” in the policy lingo) border policing to non-EU countries, which have the power to loosen their borders whenever they choose. We’ve seen versions of Ceuta happen before: in 2021, Morocco allowed 10,000 people to cross into the territory during a diplomatic row with Spain. Turkey tried something similar on Greece in 2020, and Poland has long accused Belarus (a close ally of Russia) of encouraging migrants to cross into the Schengen area.

The EU has taken an increasingly hardline stance on migration since 2015. This has paradoxically helped to create some of the problems that politicians say they’re trying to solve. The fortification of security means that people are forced into taking illegal and unsafe routes where there might have been safe, legal routes previously. When border security is breached, it results in a sudden influx of people, and the kind of alarming images that we’ve seen this week, which are then used to justify even further restrictions. “The performance of control very often leads to precisely the sense in which things are out of control,” says Trilling.

How is the right capitalising on this?

Following the events in Ceuta, Nigel Farage wasted no time in resurrecting his pernicious “Breaking Point” poster from 2016, and he and Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson, have described those who made the crossing as “fighting-age males.” The term is one of the right’s favourite new ways to frame people crossing borders, depicting them as threats, while giving little thought to those who lose their lives or don’t fit the brief. By Monday afternoon, Farage had alighted on a new policy that would use the Royal Navy to “stop the boats once and for all”. We published a useful explainer on why this would probably violate international law.

It would be possible to dismiss this announcement as a last-ditch attempt to change the subject, considering the £5m gift that Farage currently seems to want to avert eyes from (and his impending byelection bin fight). But that would be missing the bigger picture. Ceuta has given the right a powerful new argument for why hardline immigration policies are common sense, and, by contrast, why a more pragmatic and humane approach to migration is foolish, harmful or, as one Spectator piece put it recently, the result of “luxury” beliefs.

This sort of language encourages centre-left parties to accept the right’s logic. Take, for example, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who was among 22 signatories to a letter on Saturday that suggested Spain’s liberal migration policies compromise Europe’s security. These policies have no application in Ceuta, but Merz will soon be trying to fight off the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in state elections.

What happens next?

In a speech delivered from the White Cliffs of Dover on Monday, Andy Burnham pledged to be “relentless” in curbing small boats while building a system that offers “safe routes”. It marked a change from Starmer, whose attempts to appease would-be Reform voters culminated in his infamous “Island of strangers” speech. Still, it’s too early to say how Burnham will approach migration, and whether he will reopen routes that his predecessor closed.

“Time and again, the right has tried to claim that you can basically shut yourself off from the rest of the world and make these things go away,” Trilling says. “But they don’t go away. And Ceuta is a perfect example of that.”

What else we’ve been enjoying

View image in fullscreen House leaders Blanco and Samantha Escandón present laurel crowns to their campers during the opening ceremony. Photograph: Salgu Wissmath/The Guardian

I was really moved by these images from a summer camp for LGBTQ+ kids in Texas, a state where trans people have been regularly targeted and demonised. Michael

What do Feast, Viennetta, Magnum, Calippo, Twister and Cornetto have in common? They were all invented in the 15-year golden age of British ice -cream . Hettie

As a fair weather cyclist, I’ve had a smug summer, avoiding sardines-in-a-sauna style public transport on my bike. Reading about commuters on the heaving 17:46 from Euston has only confirmed this. Michael

“In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence”, the author Emily Kenway writes in this thoughtful opinion piece about the family members who sustain our care system . Hettie

I for one have (obviously) always been a fan of the Turritopsis dohrnii, but at last the immortal jellyfish is getting proper recognition in this year’s Guardian invertebrate of the year competition. Michael

The Telegraph says “Setting free Pc Harper’s killers is ‘not justice’”, the Mail writes “9,300 domestic abusers set to be released”, Metro has “Jailed just last year … but my son’s killer already set freedom”, and the Sun’s take is “See you in court, PM”.

The FT splashes “Google assembles $200bn Wall Street machine to supply chips for Anthropic”, the i Paper has “Private firms may face ban on profiteering to make care homes cheaper” and the Express writes “How many more lives will you risk by doing nothing?” The Times, on fiscal rules, says “Borrowing splurge in bid to boost economy”.

The Latest

Photograph: The Guardian

Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president?

Gianni Infantino’s reign as Fifa president is in severe peril after the collapse of his plans to sell off parts of the World Cup to private investment. Many Concacaf countries are considering following Europe’s lead by formally removing their support for Infantino, and there are widespread calls to remove him from his post. Lucy Hough speaks to columnist Jonathan Liew. Watch it on YouTube.

Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Once the soundtrack to postwar optimism and excess, Côte d’Ivoire’s dance music scene is evolving, thanks to TikTok and street dance battles.

Seven years after the death of its biggest star, DJ Arafat, a new generation of artists and dancers are reinventing the coupé-décalé genre, with the new high-energy biama movement winning over young fans and social media users alike. Eromo Egbejule visits a 400-strong neighbourhood dance arena in Abidjan, where a local rapper calls the craze “a dance for the immature”.

rss_3_1785958843.title: Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones
rss_3_1785958843.text:
Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged of about 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.

On Tuesday, as interior ministers from across the EU joined an emergency videoconference to grapple with the lingering tensions, the focus on the Moroccan side of the border with Ceuta was on the harrowing death toll.

At least 88 people have died in Ceuta, according to local officials, and another 11 in Morocco, while dozens of others remain missing.

“I have just one son,” said Hadijja, who had been waiting at the border since Saturday, scanning the steady stream of returnees for any sign of her 23-year-old son. “I haven’t had any news of him; he’s not answering his mobile phone.”

She had travelled to the border from her home in Tangier, surmising that her unemployed son was among those who had made the crossing. “He didn’t tell me he was going to cross,” she said. “This is a tragedy.”

View image in fullscreen People in Fnideq wait at the Ceuta border hoping to see their missing friends or relatives. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images

An estimated 70,000 people who arrived late last week in Ceuta had been returned to Morocco in recent days, Spain’s interior minister said Tuesday.

Referencing posts on TikTok, Facebook and WhatsApp that had claimed Morocco was letting people cross the border, people arrived at Fnideq by foot or packed into buses and cars as they joined the surge of people crossing into Spain.

Madrid sprang into action, working with Rabat to return the vast majority of those who crossed within 48 hours, even as it fended off a political crisis sparked by calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

As they returned to Moroccan soil, some said they had come home voluntarily. “I was hungry for days and filled with fear,” said Abselam, 19, from Kenitra in north-western Morocco.

A Ceuta resident had eventually taken him in, giving him food and a place to sleep, before he decided to return home. “It’s not worth it, there aren’t jobs for everyone.”

Others said they had been forced out of the Spanish territory. “The police surrounded a group of us and escorted us all the way towards the border,” said Simo, 21, from Tetuan. “We didn’t really have a choice.”

In recent days, NGOs across Spain have voiced concerns that some of those who crossed into Ceuta and who were eligible for international protection were being returned before being allowed to exercise their right to request asylum.

On Tuesday the Spanish government estimated that 2,000 people who had made the crossing were still in Ceuta. The tally includes at least 862 children who have been registered as unaccompanied minors, as Unicef Spain warned that dozens more could still be wandering the city’s streets unprotected.

“Many small children crossed over; we don’t know how many have disappeared,” Susana Hidalgo, a migration expert for the organisation, told the broadcaster TVE. The result was a “tremendously difficult” situation in Ceuta.

“There are many families on the other side of the border looking for their sons and daughters,” she said, while in Ceuta “there are 10- and 12-year-old children asking for phones so they can call their mothers and tell them they’re OK.”

Spanish police said on Tuesday they had set up an office in Ceuta to gather reports of missing people.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every fortnight Sign up to Global Dispatch Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The concerns over the fate of unaccompanied children in Ceuta were heightened on Tuesday after Spanish media published a video that appeared to show a boy age 12 crying as he begged a soldier not to send him back to Morocco. After several bystanders intervened, pointing out that Spanish law impeded children from being deported alone, the operation – which played out just metres from the border – was halted.

Days after the sudden influx, questions continue to linger as to what led to the mass crossing. Morocco has faced mounting accusations over the role it may have played. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of Ceuta, said earlier this week.

The insinuation was rejected by a senior Moroccan official. “It’s simplistic to say that Morocco should just have used force to stop them. That is to completely misunderstand this phenomenon,” the official told AFP.

“At a certain point, the Moroccan law enforcement forces could no longer confront the migrants because the numbers were very large” and because “the pull effect was very strong,” he added. “Could Spain, seeing them coming, have done something to stop them simply using weapons and security forces? That’s not possible.”

In a statement published on Sunday, Morocco’s interior ministry laid blame with the “exploitation of the digital sphere” and “the spread of misinformation” to explain the mass crossing.

Spanish intelligence sources have suggested the influx could be traced to a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported.

The Moroccan official said Rabat had sought to warn Madrid about the repercussions of the ruling. “We started engaging with the Spanish side around 22-23 July, when the networks began talking about this,” the official told AFP. “We explained that this ruling was going to create a problem. And it did create a problem.”

The claim was rejected by Spain’s migration minister, Elma Saiz. “At no point was there any evidence, any report that alerted us to the magnitude of this unprecedented event,” she told reporters in Madrid.

The uncertainty hovering over what exactly transpired extended to Fnideq, where the relatives gathered at the border spoke in hushed tones of what could have happened to their loved ones.

Many held on to hope, citing the trickle of good-news stories that had emerged in recent days, such as that of Fatima, who had spent the day waiting at the border with her family for a glimpse of her brother, who had crossed into Ceuta days earlier.

“My brother’s phone had run out of battery, but yesterday he borrowed the phone of a Spaniard to call me,” she said. “He told me he would come back this morning, so here we are waiting. I’m sure he’ll arrive soon.”

rss_4_1785958844.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says
rss_4_1785958844.text:
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.

In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”

She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spanish officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌with Morocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.

View image in fullscreen People arriving in Ceuta from Morocco last week. Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPA

Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave in north Africa on Thursday. Authorities in Ceuta reported that 88 people died trying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land borders with Africa. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.

EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.

She said the EU should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

View image in fullscreen People who arrived in Ceuta from Morocco sitting on the street. Photograph: Reduan/EPA

Italian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently said risked becoming “human rights black holes”.

The EU opened the door to offshore detention centres in June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.

Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.

The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s leader isolated.

Over the weekend, Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest” and contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.

Italy and Denmark organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision to regularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Pedro Sánchez has criticised other governments for failing to support Spain. Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/Moncloa Handout/EPA

EU member states favouring a tough approach to migration are expected to raise the issue of “pull factors” on Tuesday. “There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2 million people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open,” an EU diplomat said, referring to the approximate number of people who applied for regularisation under the 2026 Spanish government programme.

Academic research has found no evidence of a pull effect from regularisation programmes on arrivals of irregular migrants.

Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”

Amid widespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.

Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but which have been heavily criticised by rights groups.

Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”

Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”

rss_5_1785958844.title: Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media
rss_5_1785958844.text:
A popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread.

César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers.

A motorcycle with a driver and pillion rider suddenly pulled up beside them and the driver pulled out a gun and shot Gastélum at point-blank range.

A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum’s death to Reuters and said a major security operation was under way.

The killing is the latest example of bloodshed in Culiacán, which has become an epicentre of violence as factions of the Sinaloa cartel battle for control of the city.

View image in fullscreen Onlookers stand behind a police cordon at the scene of César Gastélum’s killing Photograph: Jesús Bustamante/Reuters

Mexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, said on Wednesday that authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer.

“The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference.

At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024, according to local media.

They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23, was shot and killed at a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers.

Authorities announced last week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing.

They also accused him of ordering and financing the November 2025 assassination of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan, the second largest city in Michoacán state, in a killing that shocked the country.

rss_6_1785958844.title: Peruvian cardinal hails $150m lead poisoning settlement for 1,300 people as a ‘historic milestone’
rss_6_1785958844.text:
A Peruvian cardinal who received a barrage of death threats when he challenged the firm behind a toxic smelter has called a $150m (£111m) out-of-court settlement to more than 1,000 people who were allegedly poisoned by the plant as children “a historic milestone”.

Cardinal Pedro Barreto, 82, was in Rome meeting Pope Leo XIV and other cardinals in June when he received news that the firm that ran the smelter, the Doe Run Company, a subsidiary of Renco Group, would pay $150m to 1,373 Peruvians who have suffered health impacts since childhood.

View image in fullscreen Cardinal Pedro Barreto led a campaign for justice for the Andean town of La Oroya. Photograph: Andrew Medichini/AP

The news came as Barreto – the former archbishop of Huancayo, a city in the Peruvian Andes – was preparing to travel to the US to testify in the first of four civil trials in St Louis, Missouri, as part of a 19-year legal battle against Doe Run, which is owned by US billionaire Ira Rennert, who also serves as chair of the Renco Group.

“This is a historic milestone,” said Barreto, speaking to the Guardian. “But this long-awaited justice doesn’t solve the problem faced by many children who were personally affected, especially neurologically. The money will not compensate for the harm they have suffered, but it is a sign that justice has been served.”

Barreto led a nearly two-decade campaign to hold the US company to account for the severe health impacts on the population of the Andean town of La Oroya, which the Blacksmith Institute, a US-based environmental NGO now known as Pure Earth, in 2007 listed as one of the world’s 10 most polluted places.

The settlement brought to a close one of the longest-running civil lawsuits against a multinational corporation in one country for environmental pollution or toxic exposure that caused injury or damage in another country.

Schlichter Bogard, a St Louis-based law firm, alleged that Doe Run failed to reduce lead emissions at the Peruvian multi-metal smelter, resulting in permanent injuries and harm. Doe Run Resources Corporation, which has its headquarters in St Louis, did not admit wrongdoing in agreeing to the settlement.

What began in 2007 in state court on behalf of 17 Peruvian children grew into a federal court case with more than 1,373 plaintiffs, now young adults. Each could receive at least $100,000 from the payout.

Jerry Schlichter, the founder and co-managing partner of the law firm, described the payout as a “historic tipping point in that the American companies in this case have been held responsible for their actions in another country to foreign citizens who are not US residents”.

View image in fullscreen An aerial image of the Doe Run complex and the town of La Oroya in 2022. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images

Schlichter said his team of lawyers and religious leaders such as Barreto won the settlement because of their “passion and conviction that this was a just cause, this was a righteous battle”, and that the individuals deserved their compensation for the exposure to lead emissions.

“This will be a life-changing event for every one of these 1,373 children,” Schlichter said. “It will enable them to have a new path in their life, whatever that might be.”

During his time as archbishop of Huancayo, Barreto had contacted the Saint Louis University College for Public Health and Social Justice, which sent researchers to assess the affected children in La Oroya in 2005 and found they had among some of the highest blood lead levels ever recorded. The university also found that lead, arsenic, cadmium and sulphur dioxide emissions had increased since Doe Run took over the smelting complex in 1997.

Nearly 100% of children under the age of six in La Oroya had blood-lead levels above 10 μg/dL (10 micrograms of lead in every tenth of a litre of blood), well in excess of levels that can cause growth impairment and lower IQs in children, according to a 2004 study by Peru’s environmental health office.

Barreto faced death threats and harassment, often from employees at the smelter who feared losing their livelihoods, after he began his activism in 2004, soon after taking on the archdiocese of Huancayo that includes La Oroya.

“It was an irrefutable fact that I was threatened in various ways,” said Barreto, one of three Peruvian cardinals. He said it was often done publicly and through messages that indicated that “if I kept speaking out, they were going to take much more drastic measures”.

But he stressed that it was the local population who deserved recognition.

“We have had to endure just a little of the immense suffering they constantly face,” he said.

“Before settlement, it was the longest-running case in the federal court system,” said Schlichter, who said it had been a David v Goliath fight against Rennert. “Tens of thousands of attorney hours were spent on the case and we had five national law firms who were opposing us,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Mothers wait with their children for a medical examination at La Oroya’s health clinic, 2013. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

The Department of Justice joined the defendants in asking that the lawsuit be transferred to Peru, but Schlichter resolutely opposed. “If the case had gone to Peru, the children would have got nothing,” he said. Winning the settlement was “very gratifying after such a long and risky fight”, he added.

The New York-based Renco Group and its founder, Rennert, 92, made a fortune in the 1980s junk-bond market before developing an empire of mining companies, smelting plants and industrial firms. According to Forbes in 2024, his worth is estimated at $3.8bn (£2.8bn).

In a statement, Doe Run’s chief executive, Matt Wohl, said: “We elected to put this behind us and focus on what matters – running our business, serving our customers and investing in new technologies.”

rss_7_1785958844.title: Mexico’s top university orders 58,000 students to resit entrance exam after suspected cheating
rss_7_1785958844.text:
Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university has announced that about 58,000 students will have to resit their entrance exam after abnormally high test results raised suspicions of widespread cheating.

The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam) said the exam would take place in person after its first attempt at a fully remote online version led to a debacle and thousands of annulled results.

“The Unam, the home of science, humanities and understanding, knows how to recognie mistakes and self-correct,” the university’s rector, Leonardo Lomelí, said on Monday. “There is no evasion or complacency. There is responsibility and we act accordingly.”

Nearly 160,000 students took the entrance exam earlier this summer. The at-home test included an AI-powered webcam to monitor candidates with voice and facial recognition to ensure no cheating took place. But the results indicated that the checks had failed to stop fraud.

Between 2021 and 2025 only 3.5% of applicants obtained a score of 100 or more out of 120, but this year the figure was 16%. The proportion of students who achieved a score of 110 or more increased sixfold from 0.9% to 5.5%.

Almost 30% of candidates for the medicine programme, among the most competitive undergraduate tracks in the region, obtained a score of 100 or more, compared with 9% last year.

View image in fullscreen Unam’s central library in Mexico City. Photograph: David R Frazier Photolibrary, Inc./Alamy

The results sparked a national scandal, leading the country’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, to suggest the country’s attorney general may have to investigate. “Support is always available, but in any case if a crime has been committed it is a matter for the prosecutor’s office,” she said.

Hundreds of Unam applicants protested in Mexico City on Monday against having to take the control exam, blocking major thoroughfares in the south of the capital.

Lomelí said: “I offer an apology to the candidates who, having been fairly accepted, will be called upon to take the control exam. However, it is necessary to ensure certainty and guarantee equity in access.”

The drive for more equitable access led the university to offer the exam online for the first time this year. Students previously had to travel to Mexico City from their home states, sometimes many hundreds of miles away.

The entrance exam is notoriously competitive. The more than 150,000 applicants this year were competing for 21,962 places.

Just before the results were to be publicly released, the university announced it had annulled the results of 2% of tests – 3,174 exams – after detecting irregularities such as identity impersonation, external assistance and the use of AI.

A technical expert who reviewed the results told the New York Times (NYT) that nearly half of the exams – 75,000 tests – could have involved some degree of cheating. AI may have played a role, but test questions were also leaked and even sold online while the exam was open in May and June.

Cheating tips were also widely passed around before the test went live, according to the NYT.

The Unam announced in July that it had filed a criminal complaint after detecting the alleged irregularities. It said authorities would investigate potential misconduct involving individuals or companies that allegedly offered fraudulent services to applicants and their families.

The cheating scandal compelled the institution to halt all admissions and appoint a technical committee to decide the fate of the 158,712 young people who took the exam, an unprecedented measure in the university’s 115-year modern history.

Lomelí also announced that the academic year for new students would begin on 31 August, rather than 10 August as originally scheduled.

rss_8_1785958844.title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
rss_8_1785958844.text:
Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.

The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said.

The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.”

The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump.

Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.”

Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October.

The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country.

“President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.”

The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides.

The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression.

Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time.

Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”.

The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.

The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region.

Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met.

Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family.

The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government.

Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.

rss_9_1785958844.title: Guatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of people
rss_9_1785958844.text:
Hundreds of people living on the slopes of Guatemala’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.

Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning.

By Tuesday, rivers of lava were streaming down the 3,763-metre (12,346-foot) volcano, which is located less than 100 kilometres (62 miles) from Guatemala City. Ash rose six kilometres (3.73 miles) into the red sky.

“Since early morning it was active. That night, the alarm was raised that we needed to evacuate,” a local resident, Alejandro Garcia, 68, told AFP.

Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, Garcia said, describing terrifying scenes of lava tumbling down the mountainside.

Firefighters said they transported at least 350 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality.

Evacuees are staying in a community hall, where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown.

“If there were any chance of moving to a different house, it would be better, because you’re always afraid since the volcano doesn’t give any warning,” Lidia Ortiz, 40, said at the shelter.

Escuintla, to the south, was sheltering dozens more families, including children, local authorities reported.

“If an evacuation is ordered or conditions pose a risk to your life, follow the principle of self-evacuation,” Conred spokesperson Valeria Urizar said in a video posted on social media.

The country’s Institute of Volcanology warned of hot volcanic debris flows down Fuego’s slopes, with communities on the western and southern flanks at the greatest risk.

Fuego had been erupting for 23 hours straight by Tuesday morning, it said, although the intensity was easing.

“We’ve already gotten used to having the volcano constantly active, but this time it was really too much,” 50-year-old resident Sonia Vasquez said.

Guatemalan authorities urged “precautions with air traffic”, but there has so far been no impact on the capital’s international airport.

The education ministry ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes in communities within two municipalities near the volcano.

Traffic police also closed a road encircling the mountain range that connects the south coast with the colonial city of Antigua, the country’s main tourist destination and a Unesco World Heritage site.

Guatemala lies on the Pacific ‘ring of fire’ and experiences frequent seismic and volcanic activity.

There have been several such mass evacuations in recent years because Fuego erupted.

Authorities evacuated more than 500 people last year after Fuego spurted gas and ash, with residents moved to shelters from communities near the crater.

Another eruption in 2023 pushed around 1,200 people to evacuate.

In 2018, 215 people were killed and a similar number left missing when rivers of lava poured down Fuego’s slopes and destroyed a village.
